cards.back: Change in concentration of a reactant/product per unit time (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹) — tangent slope on a concentration–time graph.
Reaction needs collisions with energy ≥ Eᴀ AND correct orientation. Both requirements together explain why so few collisions react.
Increase rate: higher temperature, higher concentration/pressure, greater surface area (powder), catalyst. None of these changes ΔH.
Energy distribution of molecules: area = total number; only the tail beyond Eᴀ reacts. Higher T flattens/shifts right; a catalyst moves the Eᴀ line left.
Provides an alternative pathway with lower Eᴀ. Regenerated unchanged; speeds both directions; no effect on ΔH or K.
In a closed system: forward rate = reverse rate, concentrations constant (not equal). Both reactions still occurring.
K = products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient. Pure solids and liquids are omitted from the expression.
K ≫ 1 → products favoured; K ≪ 1 → reactants favoured. K's size says nothing about RATE.
A system at equilibrium shifts to OPPOSE a change: concentration, pressure (fewer gas moles) or temperature (endothermic direction absorbs heat).
Higher pressure shifts toward fewer gas moles (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃: right). Inert gas at constant volume: no shift.
Shifts in the endothermic direction. For exothermic forward reactions, heating lowers the yield AND decreases K. Only T changes K.

cards.front: Why does the Haber process run at ~450 °C?
cards.back: Rate/yield compromise: forward reaction is exothermic (lower T = more NH₃) but unacceptably slow. 450 °C + Fe catalyst + high pressure.

cards.front: Why remove NH₃ continuously in industry?
cards.back: Liquefying and removing product keeps Q < K → equilibrium keeps shifting forward → more production.

cards.front: Q vs K — what does Q < K mean?
cards.back: Too few products relative to equilibrium → forward shift until Q = K. Q > K → reverse shift.
Catalyst = faster, NOT more product. Inert gas at constant volume = no shift. 'Equal concentrations' at equilibrium = false (equal RATES).

cards.front: Where does the temperature effect bite in the Haber process?
cards.back: K itself decreases as T rises (exothermic forward). Every other stress shifts position without changing K.
Give the direction AND the Le Châtelier justification (opposing the change). Direction alone = half marks.
Read tangents for initial rate, compare curves for T/conc changes, and explain with collision theory + the MB tail — not just 'molecules move faster'.

cards.front: Why is kinetics about the JOURNEY and equilibrium about the DESTINATION?
cards.back: Kinetics: how fast equilibrium is reached (Eᴀ, pathway). Equilibrium: where the mixture ends up (K, thermodynamics). Catalysts touch only the journey.
